Plato, however, denied that this omniscience could ever be attained. From his point of view, “dogmatics” must therefore always be submitted, again and again, to dialectical treatment. In any case, Plato draws a very clear distinction between dialectic and dogmatics. In his dialogues he never gives an explicit answer to the problem under discussion: thesis and antithesis remain without a synthesis. Yet the answer—the synthesis—is contained within them, and the reader must work it out personally from the dialectical process that has been presented.
This emphasizes that the answer, meaning the synthesis or knowledge, lies outside dialectic. It already belongs to “dogmatics,” which Plato himself presented in his lost work On the Good.

It is easy to see that Plato’s dialectical method is analogous to the method used by physics, especially modern physics. By varying the coordinate system, physics rejects whatever is “valid” only within one particular system. Whatever remains unchanged under all these changes is regarded as true—that is, as corresponding to reality.

Dialectic does the same thing. It rejects whatever is “valid” only from the standpoint of one possible opinion. It treats as knowledge only what remains after this purification: what is valid from the standpoint of all possible opinions.
“Knowledge,” therefore, is nothing other than the invariant of “opinions.”

97) This is especially easy to see in Plotinus, who regarded himself as Plato’s successor but clearly failed to understand what Platonic dialectic was. At the beginning of Christian philosophy, however, we see the idea of dialectic revived, especially in Augustine. Later, at the beginning of modern bourgeois philosophy, Descartes revived it again, just as Hegel would revive it at the beginning of socialist philosophy.
Augustine knows that truth can be reached only through dialogue. But he does not speak with another human being; he speaks with God.

In one sense, this is a step backward. It obscures the social character of dialectic and indirectly prepares the way for Descartes’s solitary dialectic, which Descartes inherits from Augustine after dismissing God.

But in another sense it is a step forward. Augustine’s interaction with God does not consist only in discourse. It also contains elements beyond discourse and beyond reason: faith, love, prayer, ritual, the life of the righteous, and so on.

This indirectly prepares the way for Hegel’s correct understanding of dialectic as an active process. In Hegel, God is once again replaced by humanity—but not by isolated, accidental individuals, as in Plato. He is replaced by humanity in the full course of its historical development.
In one sense, Plato and Augustine are merely the thesis and antithesis from which the Hegelian synthesis emerges:
human–discourse, God–action, human–action; isolated individual, universal God, universal humanity.

Any action that goes against the existing interests of a society without aiming to change that society must be regarded as absolutely criminal. This is the case, for example, with theft that benefits only the thief or murder that concerns only the murderer.
By contrast, theft or murder carried out in the service of a revolutionary idea may be a mistake, but it is not a crime.

The same applies to madness. Anyone who rejects the fundamental truths commonly accepted by society, while making no effort to produce arguments capable of persuading others of the contrary, must be regarded as insane.
In this sense, every “utopian” comes fairly close to madness, if by “utopia” we mean a revolutionary political project that gives no indication of the means by which it could actually be realized.
A political project is revolutionary rather than utopian only when it takes the existing conditions into account and shows how one can begin from them and arrive at a new order.
Only such a project deserves to be discussed, because only such a project can be verified through revolution.

119) There is no contradiction here with what I said earlier about “social verification.”

The philosopher, as a philosopher, cannot set his own opinions against what the society to which he belongs regards as true—provided that this society is not prerevolutionary, meaning destined to disappear.
But first, he must know why he behaves in this way. Second, he must know who the legitimate representative of that society and State is.
He therefore does not submit to this representative as an individual, but to the society that the representative represents.

At present, the legitimate representative of Soviet society as a whole is unquestionably Comrade Stalin. To the extent that Comrade Stalin acts as the representative of that society, his judgment is therefore binding on the Soviet philosopher.
But the philosopher does not accept this judgment simply because Joseph Vissarionovich has said it. Joseph Vissarionovich’s personal opinion is just as suspect as any opinion whatsoever.

Here again we can appeal to the Christian tradition. The Catholic Church draws the same distinction between the Pope’s personal opinion, which may be questioned, and what he says ex cathedra—that is, in his capacity as the representative of the Church—which is not open to dispute.
The error in that case is simply this: the Pope’s authority is supposedly based on “God,” whereas the authority of the leader of Soviet society is consciously and openly based on that society itself.
And if it can be shown that, for the present, this society is the truest one, then the truth of the “authorities” it recognizes has thereby also been shown and proved.

We thus arrive at a kind of “circular guarantee.” By recognizing a given philosophy, society guarantees its “sociohistorical truth”—that is, it guarantees that this philosophy corresponds to the social realities of the historical period in question.

And the philosophy recognized by society, in turn, guarantees the “sociohistorical truth” of that society by showing that, under the given historical conditions, it is the most fully realized society—or, more precisely, the only society that is actually possible: a stable, postrevolutionary society rather than a prerevolutionary one.
